---
title: "Coverage Fundamentals: Zones, Leverage, and Reading the Shell"
subtitle: "The names coaches give the grass, how a defender lines up on a receiver, the three ways to guard one, and how to read the safeties before the ball is snapped."
description: "The vocabulary every coverage chapter is built on: the underneath zones (flat, curl, hook, hole) and the deep layer (thirds, halves, quarters) with their landmarks; press, off and bail alignments, cushion, trail technique and eye discipline; spot-drop zone, pattern matching and man coverage on the same routes; reading the shell (middle of the field closed or open, safety depth and width); the Cover 0-9 numbering and its dialects, including Cover 7, 8 and 9; and how the 5-yard contact rule shapes it all."
glossary:
  "Flat zone": "The short area near the sideline, from the line of scrimmage to about 6 or 7 yards deep and from roughly the slot or the numbers out to the sideline: where flat routes, quick outs and swing passes are caught."
  "Curl zone": "The intermediate area between the hash marks and the numbers, centred about 10 to 12 yards deep, where curls, deep hitches and in-breaking routes from wide receivers arrive."
  "Hook zone": "The short-to-intermediate area inside the curl zone, around the hash marks and over the offensive tackles, about 5 to 12 yards deep; the linebackers' home in most zone coverages."
  "Hole zone": {def: "The middle of the field in front of the deep middle defender, roughly 8 to 15 yards deep between the hash marks, where digs and crossing routes arrive. Some staffs reserve 'rat' for a lower spot in the same lane, 5 to 8 yards deep.", aliases: ["Rat zone"]}
  "Deep third": "One of three deep zones, each a third of the field's width (about 18 yards), guarded by the two cornerbacks and a deep middle safety in Cover 3."
  "Deep half": "One of two deep zones, each half the field's width (about 27 yards), guarded by a safety in Cover 2 and its relatives."
  "Deep quarter": "One of four deep zones, each about 13 yards wide, guarded by the two cornerbacks and the two safeties in quarters (Cover 4)."
  Press: "Lining a cornerback (or another defender) up within about a yard of a receiver, to jam him with the hands at the snap and knock his route off its timing. Contact is legal only until the receiver is 5 yards past the line of scrimmage."
  "Off coverage": "Lining a defender up several yards (usually 5 to 10) away from his receiver, so he can give ground at the snap and keep the receiver in front of him."
  Bail: "A cornerback technique: at the snap, turn the hips and run to a deep landmark instead of backpedalling. Used from off alignments every week; from a press look ('press-bail') it also makes a zone coverage look like man before the snap."
  Cushion: "The distance, in yards of depth, between a defender and the receiver he is covering. A big cushion protects against the deep ball and concedes the short throw."
  "Trail technique": "A man-coverage position in which the defender runs a step behind and underneath his receiver, on his hip, to take away short and in-breaking throws, trusting a safety to help over the top."
  Landmark: "A spot on the field (a depth plus a width keyed to the hash marks, the numbers or a receiver) that a zone defender aims for on his drop, so that the zones are spaced the same way on every play."
  "Spot-drop zone": "Zone coverage in which each defender drops to a fixed landmark and then reacts to the quarterback's eyes and the throw, guarding his area rather than any particular receiver."
  "Pattern matching": "Zone coverage in which defenders read the receivers' routes as they develop and pick up, man to man, whoever enters or stays in their area, passing receivers from one defender to the next by rule. Most NFL zone coverage today matches to some degree."
  MOFC: {def: "Middle of the field closed: a defense with one deep safety in the middle of the field (a one-high shell, as in Cover 1 and Cover 3), so the deep middle is guarded.", aliases: ["Middle of field closed"]}
  MOFO: {def: "Middle of the field open: a defense with nobody in the deep middle, usually because two safeties split the field between them (a two-high shell, as in Cover 2 and quarters).", aliases: ["Middle of field open"]}
  "Coverage numbering (Cover 0-9)": "The naming convention behind 'Cover 0' to 'Cover 9'. Through Cover 4 the number usually counts the deep defenders; from 5 up the numbers are names, and their meaning differs from staff to staff."
  "Cover 8": "A rarely used number with no standard meaning. In Vic Fangio's vocabulary it is a split-field coverage, quarters on one side and Cover 2 on the other (what most teams call Cover 6); other staffs use 8 for other calls."
  "Cover 9": "A number with several meanings: a Cover 3 in which the safety away from the offense's strength comes down (weak rotation) on some staffs, Cover 3 match or a split-field call on others. The FTN charting in nflverse has labelled plays COVER_9 since 2023."
  "Eye discipline": "Looking at the right thing at the right moment: a zone defender's eyes on the quarterback and his key receivers, a man defender's on his man. Many big plays against sound coverage start with a defender's eyes in the wrong place."
---

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (shared drawing helpers for this chapter)"
#| output: false
import os
import logging
import shutil

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Circle, Ellipse, FancyArrowPatch, FancyBboxPatch, Rectangle, RegularPolygon, Patch
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D

import gridiron.play as gplay
from gridiron import Play, Player, Field, style, draw_marker, routes as r

logging.getLogger("matplotlib.font_manager").setLevel(logging.ERROR)
style.apply()
PDF = os.environ.get("RTG_FORMAT", "").lower() in ("pdf", "typst", "print")

HALF = 80 / 3            # yards from the middle of the field to either sideline (26.7)
HASH_W = 18.5 / 6        # NFL hash marks: 18 ft 6 in apart, so 3.1 yards either side of the middle
NUM_W = HALF - 12.0      # the painted numbers start 12 yards in from the sideline: 14.7 from the middle
GREEN_TEXT = "#0f7a55"   # a darker step of the green highlight, for text on the light field
DD = style.DEFENSE_DARK
GREY = style.MUTED


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- players and alignments
def O(key, pos, d, w, label=None):
    return Player(key, pos, "off", d, w, label=key if label is None else label)


def D(key, pos, d, w, label):
    return Player(key, pos, "def", d, w, label=label)


def line5():
    """The five offensive linemen, 1.6 yards apart (only the center is lettered)."""
    return [O(k, k, -0.7, w, "C" if k == "C" else "") for k, w in
            (("LT", -3.2), ("LG", -1.6), ("C", 0.0), ("RG", 1.6), ("RT", 3.2))]


def spread():
    """11 personnel, shotgun 2x2: X and Z on the line (with the five linemen: seven on the line),
    H in the left slot and the tight end Y flexed into the right slot, both a step off the ball."""
    return line5() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -1.5, "R"),
                      O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0), O("H", "WR", -1.5, -9.0),
                      O("Y", "TE", -1.5, 9.0), O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 15.0)]


def front4():
    return [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -5.6, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.8, "T"),
            D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.4, "T"), D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 5.6, "E")]


def nickel(**spots):
    """4-2-5 nickel against the 2x2. Defaults are a neutral two-high look; pass KEY=(d, w) to move
    anyone (keys: MIKE, WILL, NB, LCB, RCB, FS, SS)."""
    base = {"MIKE": (4.5, 1.8), "WILL": (4.5, -2.2), "NB": (5.0, -7.4), "LCB": (7.0, -16.0),
            "RCB": (7.0, 16.0), "FS": (12.5, -8.5), "SS": (12.5, 8.5)}
    base.update(spots)
    lab = {"MIKE": ("MIKE", "M"), "WILL": ("WILL", "W"), "NB": ("NB", "$"), "LCB": ("CB", "CB"),
           "RCB": ("CB", "CB"), "FS": ("FS", "FS"), "SS": ("SS", "SS")}
    return front4() + [D(k, lab[k][0], *base[k], lab[k][1]) for k in base]


def protect(p, rushers=("WDE", "WDT", "SDT", "SDE"), linemen=("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT")):
    """Linemen set, four rushers engage them: enough to say 'pass', no more."""
    for k in linemen:
        if k in p.players:
            p.block(k, pts=[(-1.2, 0.0)])
    for k in rushers:
        if k in p.players:
            p.rush(k, pts=[(-1.6, 0.0)], speed=2.0)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- drawing helpers
def P(fld, p, d, w):
    return fld.xy(*p.to_abs(d, w))


def clean(ax):
    """Drop the painted yard numbers (they sit where receivers stand); clip text to the window."""
    for t in list(ax.texts):
        if t.get_alpha() == 0.55:
            t.remove()
        else:
            t.set_clip_on(True)


def ruler(fld, p, fs=6.0, step=5, top=40):
    """Depth labels (yards past the line of scrimmage) just inside the left edge of the window."""
    xl = (160 / 3) - fld.y1 + 0.4
    for d in range(step, top + 1, step):
        y = p.los + d
        if fld.x0 + 1.5 <= y <= fld.x1 - 1.5:
            fld.ax.text(xl, y, f"{d}" + (" yd" if d == step else ""), fontsize=fs, color=style.INK_2,
                        ha="left", va="center", zorder=12,
                        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.12", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.85))


def widths(fld, p, d, fs=6.0, which=("hash", "numbers")):
    """Italic 'hash' and 'numbers' markers at depth d, wherever they fall inside the window."""
    spots = []
    if "hash" in which:
        spots += [(-HASH_W, "hash"), (HASH_W, "hash")]
    if "numbers" in which:
        spots += [(-NUM_W, "numbers"), (NUM_W, "numbers")]
    for w, txt in spots:
        x, y = P(fld, p, d, w)
        if fld.y0 + 2.5 <= p.ball_y - w <= fld.y1 - 2.5:
            fld.ax.text(float(x), float(y), txt, fontsize=fs, color=style.INK_2, ha="center", va="center",
                        style="italic", zorder=12,
                        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.12", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.85))


def say(fld, p, d, w, text, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=7.0, ha="center", weight="normal", box=True):
    x, y = P(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.text(float(x), float(y), text, fontsize=fontsize, color=color, ha=ha, va="center", zorder=13,
                fontweight=weight, linespacing=1.15,
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.18", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.9) if box else None)


def point_to(fld, p, text_at, target, text, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=7.0, ha="center"):
    (xt, yt), (xp, yp) = P(fld, p, *text_at), P(fld, p, *target)
    fld.ax.annotate(text, (float(xp), float(yp)), xytext=(float(xt), float(yt)), fontsize=fontsize,
                    color=color, ha=ha, va="center", zorder=13, linespacing=1.15,
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=color, lw=0.7, shrinkA=2, shrinkB=7),
                    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.18", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.9))


def dim(fld, p, a, b, text, text_at, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=6.8):
    """A dimension line between two (d, w) points, labelled at text_at."""
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = P(fld, p, *a), P(fld, p, *b)
    fld.ax.annotate("", (float(x1), float(y1)), xytext=(float(x0), float(y0)),
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color=color, lw=0.8, shrinkA=0, shrinkB=0), zorder=6)
    say(fld, p, *text_at, text, color=color, fontsize=fontsize)


def zone_box(fld, p, d0, d1, w0, w1, label="", color=style.DEFENSE, alpha=0.12, fs=7.0, ls=(0, (3, 2))):
    """A rounded, shaded rectangle from depth d0 to d1 and width w0 to w1 (yards), labelled in the middle."""
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = P(fld, p, d0, w0), P(fld, p, d1, w1)
    lo_x, lo_y = float(min(x0, x1)), float(min(y0, y1))
    fld.ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((lo_x, lo_y), float(abs(x1 - x0)), float(abs(y1 - y0)),
                                    boxstyle="round,pad=0,rounding_size=1.2", fc=color, alpha=alpha,
                                    ec="none", zorder=1.5))
    fld.ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((lo_x, lo_y), float(abs(x1 - x0)), float(abs(y1 - y0)),
                                    boxstyle="round,pad=0,rounding_size=1.2", fc="none", ec=color, lw=0.9,
                                    ls=ls, zorder=1.6))
    if label:
        say(fld, p, (d0 + d1) / 2, (w0 + w1) / 2, label, color=style.INK, fontsize=fs, box=False)


def path(fld, p, pts, color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.4, dash=(0, (3, 2)), z=5):
    """A dashed arrow through absolute (d, w) points."""
    xs, ys = P(fld, p, np.array([q[0] for q in pts]), np.array([q[1] for q in pts]))
    fld.ax.plot(xs, ys, color=color, lw=lw, ls=dash, zorder=z, solid_capstyle="round")
    fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((xs[-2], ys[-2]), (xs[-1], ys[-1]), arrowstyle="-|>",
                                     mutation_scale=9, color=color, lw=lw, zorder=z))


def ghost(fld, p, d, w, label="", color=style.DEFENSE):
    """A hollow, dashed defender: where he stood before he moved."""
    x, y = P(fld, p, d, w)
    ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
    fld.ax.add_patch(RegularPolygon((float(x), float(y)), 4, radius=gplay.MARKER_R * 1.25, orientation=np.pi / 4,
                                    fc="none", ec=color, lw=1.1, ls=(0, (2, 1.2)), zorder=6))
    if label:
        fld.ax.text(float(x), float(y), label, ha="center", va="center", color=color, fontweight="bold",
                    zorder=6, fontsize=max(4.0, min(8.5, ppy * 0.75)))


def panel_title(ax, text, fs=8.5):
    ax.set_title(text, fontsize=fs, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")


def draw(p, ax=None, lateral="full", window=(-8.5, 22), width_in=6.5, show_ruler=True, rfs=6.0):
    fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=lateral, window=window, width_in=width_in, title=False)
    clean(fld.ax)
    if show_ruler:
        ruler(fld, p, fs=rfs)
    return fld


LEGEND = {
    "route": Line2D([], [], color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.8, label="route"),
    "drop": Line2D([], [], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (3, 2)), label="defender's movement"),
    "ghost": Patch(fc="none", ec=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.1, ls=(0, (2, 1.2)), label="where he lined up"),
    "ring": Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", ms=11, mfc="none", mec=style.THIRD, mew=2, label="watch him"),
    "zone": Patch(fc=style.DEFENSE, alpha=0.18, ec=style.DEFENSE, ls=(0, (3, 2)), label="zone"),
    "pass": Line2D([], [], color=style.BALL, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (2, 2)), label="the throw"),
    "ltg": Line2D([], [], color=style.LINE_TO_GAIN, lw=2.2, label="line to gain"),
}


def field_legend(ax, keys, fs=7.0, ncol=None):
    hs = [LEGEND[k] for k in keys]
    ax.legend(handles=hs, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 0.0), ncol=ncol or min(len(hs), 4),
              fontsize=fs, frameon=False, handlelength=2.0, columnspacing=1.2, borderaxespad=0.2)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- moments of a simulated play
def set_track(p, key, rows):
    """Hand-made keyframes [(t, d, w), ...] for one player (zone reads and man shadowing that
    gridiron's straight-line drop() and man() can't express). Call after every other action."""
    kf, t0, t1 = p._compile()
    kf = dict(kf)
    q = p.players[key]
    rows = [(min(t0, -1.0), q.d, q.w), (0.0, q.d, q.w)] + [tuple(x) for x in rows]
    kf[key] = np.array(rows, dtype=float)
    p._compiled = (kf, t0, max(t1, rows[-1][0]))


def shadow(p, key, target, off, lag=0.3, t_on=0.9, t_from=0.0, start=None, t_end=3.0):
    """Keyframes for a defender who leaves `start` (or his alignment) at t_from and settles
    `off` = (down, right) yards from where `target` was `lag` seconds earlier, fully by t_on."""
    q = p.players[key]
    s = np.array(start if start is not None else (q.d, q.w), dtype=float)
    rows = []
    for tt in np.round(np.arange(t_from + 0.05, t_end + 1e-9, 0.05), 3):
        f = min(1.0, max(0.0, (tt - t_from) / max(1e-6, t_on - t_from)))
        f = f * f * (3 - 2 * f)
        tgt = p.position(target, max(0.0, tt - lag)) + np.array(off)
        rows.append((tt, *(s * (1 - f) + tgt * f)))
    return rows


def moment(ax, p, t, lateral, window, rings=(), throw_t=None, label_fs=None):
    """Everyone at time t, with faint trails of where they have been and the ball's flight so far."""
    ylo, yhi = sorted((p.ball_y - lateral[0], p.ball_y - lateral[1]))
    fld = Field(ax=ax, orient="vertical", los=p.los, window=window, numbers=False, lateral=(ylo, yhi),
                to_go=None)
    ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
    inside = lambda d, w: (window[0] + 0.6 <= d <= window[1] - 0.6) and (lateral[0] + 0.6 <= w <= lateral[1] - 0.6)  # noqa: E731
    for k, q in p.players.items():
        if q.pos in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT", "DE", "DT"):
            continue
        pts = np.array([p.position(k, tt) for tt in np.linspace(0.0, max(t, 0.0), 40)])
        if t > 0 and np.ptp(pts[:, 0]) + np.ptp(pts[:, 1]) > 0.3:
            xs, ys = P(fld, p, pts[:, 0], pts[:, 1])
            ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.OFFENSE if q.side == "off" else style.DEFENSE,
                    lw=1.0, alpha=0.55, zorder=3, ls="-" if q.side == "off" else (0, (3, 2)))
    if throw_t is not None and t > throw_t:
        b = np.array([p.ball_position(tt) for tt in np.linspace(throw_t, t, 25)])
        xs, ys = P(fld, p, b[:, 0], b[:, 1])
        ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.BALL, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (2, 1.5)), zorder=9)
    for k, q in p.players.items():
        d, w = p.position(k, t)
        if not inside(d, w):
            continue
        x, y = P(fld, p, d, w)
        draw_marker(ax, float(x), float(y), q.side, q.label, ppy, ring=style.THIRD if k in rings else None)
    if t > 0.05:
        bd, bw = p.ball_position(t)
        if inside(bd, bw):
            # in the quarterback's hand: beside him; thrown: just upfield of the ball, so letters stay readable
            bx, by = P(fld, p, *((bd, bw - 1.0) if t <= (throw_t or 99) else (bd + 1.2, bw)))
            ax.add_patch(Ellipse((float(bx), float(by)), 1.0, 0.62, fc=style.BALL, ec="white", lw=0.5, zorder=11))
    return fld


def tag(fld, p, t, text, fs=6.6):
    """A caption tucked in the bottom-left corner of a frame panel (the empty backfield)."""
    fld.ax.text(0.03, 0.03, text, transform=fld.ax.transAxes, ha="left", va="bottom", fontsize=fs,
                color=style.INK, zorder=15, linespacing=1.15,
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.25", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=0.5))
```

Second-and-8, first quarter. Before the snap, the broadcast's analyst draws a circle around a
cornerback standing eight yards away from the receiver he's supposedly guarding, and says, "Look
at that cushion. Off coverage, eyes inside. Middle of the field is closed. I'd bet Cover 3." The
quarterback takes the snap and throws a quick hitch right in front of that cornerback for six
yards. On the next play the same cornerback is standing a yard from the same receiver, nose to
nose, and the analyst says, "Now he's pressing. But watch: he'll bail." At the snap the corner
turns his back on the receiver and sprints downfield, and the quarterback, who expected man
coverage, throws a quick out into a zone, where a linebacker who never left the area knocks it down. A casual fan hears this as a stream of jargon. Why would a
defender stand so far from the player he's meant to stop? What does "the middle of the field is
closed" mean, and why does it predict a number? What *is* Cover 3? This chapter is the
vocabulary every other chapter in Part 6 is written in: the names coaches give the grass, the
ways a defender can line up on a receiver, the three ways to guard one, and how to read the
whole picture from the safeties before the ball is snapped.

**You'll be able to…**

- Point to the flat, curl, hook and hole zones on a broadcast shot, and say which deep split
  (thirds, halves or quarters) a defense is playing and what each split gives away.
- Tell press from off coverage and spot a bail, and say what each gives up: cushion, leverage,
  and where the defender's eyes are.
- Tell spot-drop zone, pattern-matching zone and man coverage apart on a replay by watching one
  defender for one second.
- Call the middle of the field closed or open at the snap, and use the safeties' depth and width
  and the corners' alignment to guess which coverage is coming.
- Decode coverage numbers from Cover 0 to Cover 9, and know when a number means different things
  to different teams.
- Explain how the 5-yard contact rule shapes the way cornerbacks play.

::: {.callout-note title="You'll need"}
- **The defense's two big pictures** ([A First Look at Defense](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd)):
  in [man coverage](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-man-coverage) each defender has a receiver;
  in [zone coverage](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-zone-coverage) each has an area. The
  [shell](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-shell-coverage-shell) is the safeties' picture before
  the snap: [one-high](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-one-high) (one deep safety in the middle)
  or [two-high](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-two-high) (one deep on each side). The
  [nickel](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-nickel) defense (five defensive backs) is the NFL's
  everyday package, and a four-man rush leaves seven defenders to cover.
- **The routes the zones are drawn against** ([Dropback Concepts](../04-the-passing-game/04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd)):
  offenses run receivers in combinations, such as
  [curl-flat](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-curl-flat), [flood](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-flood),
  [smash](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-smash) and
  [four verticals](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-four-verticals), that put two receivers on one
  defender or more deep routes than there are deep defenders. That chapter drew them from the
  offense's side; this one draws the defense they are attacking.
- **Routes and leverage** ([Passing Fundamentals](../04-the-passing-game/04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd),
  [The Quick Game](../04-the-passing-game/04-03-quick-game.qmd)): a [seam](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-seam)
  runs straight up between the hash and the numbers, a [dig](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-dig)
  breaks flat across the field at 10 to 15 yards, a [hitch](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hitch)
  stops and turns back, a [flat route](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-flat-route) runs to the
  sideline near the line. A defender's [leverage](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-leverage-inside-outside)
  is which side of the receiver he stands on: inside protects the middle, outside the sideline.
  Receivers are numbered from the sideline in: #1 is the widest on his side, then #2.
- **The field** ([The Game in Fifteen Minutes](../01-foundations/01-01-the-game-in-fifteen-minutes.qmd)):
  the NFL [hash marks](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hash-marks) sit only about 3 yards either
  side of the middle of a field 53⅓ yards wide; the painted yard-line numbers start 12 yards in
  from each sideline, about 15 yards from the middle.

*Reading the diagrams:* offense is blue circles (X, H, Y and Z receivers; Q quarterback; R running
back; C center). Defense is outlined squares: E and T the defensive ends and tackles, M and W the
Mike and Will linebackers, $ the nickel back, CB a cornerback, FS and SS the free and strong
safeties. A green ring marks the player to watch. Faint lines across the field are 5 yards apart,
starting at the line of scrimmage (the darker blue line); the small numbers on the left edge give
the depth in yards. Solid arrows are routes; dashed arrows are defenders' movements; a brown
dotted line is the ball in the air. A solid orange line across the field is the
[line to gain](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-line-to-gain) (the first-down line).
:::

## The defense's arithmetic

Start with a problem of numbers and geometry. On a typical passing down the defense rushes four
and has seven players left to guard five eligible receivers and a field 53⅓ yards wide and as
deep as the quarterback can throw. That sounds like plenty, seven against five, until you
remember that the offense chooses where its five go, and the defense has to decide where its
seven stand *before* it knows.

There are only two ways to hand out the seven. You can give each defender a person (man
coverage), or a piece of the field (zone coverage). Every coverage in the NFL is one of those, a
mixture of the two, or, increasingly, a zone that turns into man once the receivers declare
their routes. This chapter is about the vocabulary of the zone half first, because the zones are
also the map everybody, including man-coverage defenders, uses to talk about where the ball can
go.

The map has two layers, and the reason is the most important idea in pass defense. **A ball
thrown over a defender's head is worth far more than a ball caught in front of him.** A
completion in front of the defense gains what it gains and the receiver is tackled. A completion
behind the defense can be a touchdown. So every coverage first decides how many players it will
spend on the **deep** layer, guaranteeing that nobody gets behind them, and then spreads the rest
across the **underneath** layer, in front of them. That one decision, how many deep, is what the
coverage numbers count, what the safeties' alignment advertises, and what the rest of this
chapter keeps coming back to. ([Expected Points, EPA, and Success Rate](../13-analytics-and-data/13-02-expected-points-and-success-rate.qmd)
puts numbers on how much more a deep completion is worth.)

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists"}
**Zones exist because the quarterback, not the receiver, decides where the ball goes.** A
defender who watches the quarterback can react to the throw from wherever he is, and a defense
with every defender facing the quarterback can rally to the ball and tackle. **What zone gives
up** is the space *between* defenders. With seven players on a field this big there are always
seams between the zones, and much of offensive football (most of
[Dropback Concepts](../04-the-passing-game/04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd)) is the art of
putting receivers in those seams, or putting two receivers in one defender's zone so he can only
take one.
:::

## The zone map: names for the grass

Coaches carve the underneath layer into a handful of named areas. The names are old and nearly
universal, though the exact boundaries vary by team, and they are worth learning because
broadcasters use them constantly ("he's the curl-flat player," "they sat a linebacker in the
hole").

```{python}
#| label: fig-zone-map
#| fig-cap: "The zone map, drawn against a 2x2 formation with the ball in the middle of the field. Underneath, from the sideline in: the flat (shallow, near the sideline), the curl (between the numbers and the hash, about 10 to 12 yards deep), the hook (around the hash, over the tackles) and, in the middle, the hole in front of the deep defenders. The deep layer above about 15 yards is split into thirds, halves or quarters depending on the coverage (next figure). The boxes are where each zone's defender works, not walls: real zones overlap, stretch and shift with the formation and the ball's spot."
zm = Play(spread(), [], los=40, to_go=None)
fld = draw(zm, lateral="full", window=(-8.5, 32.0))
for s in (-1, 1):
    zone_box(fld, zm, 1.0, 7.0, s * 11.0, s * 23.5, "flat\n0–7 yd deep")
    zone_box(fld, zm, 7.5, 14.5, s * 6.5, s * 14.8, "curl\n~10–12 yd")
    zone_box(fld, zm, 5.0, 11.5, s * 0.7, s * 6.0, "hook\n5–12 yd")
zone_box(fld, zm, 12.0, 17.5, -4.2, 4.2, "hole (rat)")
zone_box(fld, zm, 19.0, 30.0, -24.0, 24.0, "the deep layer: split into thirds, halves or quarters",
         color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, alpha=0.06, fs=7.5)
widths(fld, zm, -7.0)
plt.show()
```

Here is what each zone is for, and why it sits where it does.

- **The [flat zone](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-flat-zone)** is the short area near the
  sideline, from the line of scrimmage to about 6 or 7 yards deep, from roughly the slot receiver
  or the numbers out to the sideline. It is where flat routes, quick outs, swing passes and
  screens are caught. Why guard it at all, when a catch there gains only a few yards? Because an
  unguarded flat is an *easy* few yards: a completion on every snap moves the chains. The
  defender who has it is usually a cornerback (in Cover 2), a nickel back or an outside
  linebacker.
- **The [curl zone](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-curl-zone)** sits between the numbers and
  the hash, centred about 10 to 12 yards deep. It is named for the route a wide receiver runs
  into it: push up the field, stop, turn back inside. It is the first throw past the sticks on
  most third downs, which is why the defender who has it matters so much.
- **The [hook zone](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hook-zone)** is inside the curl, around the
  hash and over the offensive tackles, about 5 to 12 yards deep: the linebackers' home. Tight ends
  and slot receivers "hook up" (stop and turn) here, and it is the lane of the quick in-breaking
  routes.
- **The [hole zone](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hole-zone)** is the middle of the field in
  front of the deep defenders, roughly 8 to 15 yards deep between the hashes. Digs and crossing
  routes arrive here, so a defender sitting in the hole (often called a
  [rat](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-rat-zone), or a [robber](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-robber)
  when it's a safety coming down) is aiming at the most valuable intermediate throws on the field.
  Usage of "rat" varies: some staffs mean any hole player, others a defender sitting lower, 5 to 8
  yards deep, under the crossing routes.

Notice how few defenders that leaves. There are seven underneath areas on the map (two flats, two
curls, two hooks, the hole), and with four rushers and three deep defenders, there are only four
players to cover them. That isn't a design flaw. It's the trade every coverage makes, and it's
why defenders are taught to cover *two* areas each, as "curl-flat" or "hook-curl" players,
starting in one and sliding to the other as the routes develop.

What makes him slide? Take the curl-flat defender. He drops first toward the curl, because the
curl is the deeper and more dangerous throw, and he keeps his eyes on the quarterback while
feeling the receivers around him: the outside receiver (#1) threatening the curl behind him, the
inside one (#2) heading for the flat in front of him. When the quarterback looks to the flat, or
the ball is thrown there, he breaks down to it; until then he sits under the curl. That is the
dilemma the [curl-flat](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-curl-flat) concept builds on purpose: one
receiver in each of his two areas, and the quarterback throws to whichever one he doesn't take.
A flat throw is the one he can afford to give up, because he arrives as the ball does and tackles
for a short gain.

### Landmarks: how a zone stays the same shape

A zone defender doesn't drop to "somewhere around the curl." He drops to a
**[landmark](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-landmark)**: a spot defined by a depth and a width
keyed to something on the field. "Twelve yards deep, top of the numbers." "Ten yards, inside
shoulder of #1." "Deep middle, 18 yards, splitting the hashes." Landmarks exist for the same
reason a choreographer marks the stage: if every defender hits his spot, the gaps between the
zones are the size the coach planned, on every snap, wherever the ball is spotted. A defender who
drifts two yards off his landmark opens a window two yards wider for somebody else's receiver.
Landmarks are also what receivers aim at from the other side: seams two yards outside the hash,
go routes on the numbers ([Dropback Concepts](../04-the-passing-game/04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd)
lists them). Offense and defense are aiming at the same painted lines.

Landmarks move with the ball. With the ball on a hash, the short side of the field (the
[boundary](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-boundary-side)) is about 23½ yards wide and the
[wide side](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-field-side) about 30, so a deep third to the boundary
is narrower than one to the field, and many teams play different coverages to the two sides for
exactly that reason ([Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage](06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd)).
Most snaps on a broadcast look like this, not like the tidy middle-of-the-field map above.

```{python}
#| label: fig-zone-map-hash
#| fig-cap: "The same underneath map with the ball on the offense's left hash, the usual broadcast picture. The zones are keyed to the paint, so they slide with the ball: the boundary (short) side is squeezed into about 23½ yards and its flat is small, while the field (wide) side stretches across about 30, with a wide flat that a single defender struggles to cover."
zh = Play(spread(), [], los=40, ball_y="left", to_go=None)
fld = draw(zh, lateral="full", window=(-8.5, 19.0))
MB = -HASH_W                      # the ball is a hash-width left of the middle


def zh_box(d0, d1, m0, m1, lab):
    """Zone box with widths given from the middle of the field (m), drawn relative to the ball."""
    zone_box(fld, zh, d0, d1, m0 - MB, m1 - MB, lab, fs=6.6)


zh_box(1.0, 7.0, -14.0, -25.2, "flat")
zh_box(7.5, 14.5, -9.0, -15.5, "curl")
zh_box(5.0, 11.5, -3.6, -8.5, "hook")
zh_box(5.0, 11.5, -2.6, 3.4, "hook")
zh_box(7.5, 14.5, 3.9, 15.5, "curl")
zh_box(1.0, 7.0, 12.0, 25.2, "flat")
zh_box(12.0, 17.5, -7.0, 1.0, "hole")
dim(fld, zh, (-6.6, -HALF - MB + 0.2), (-6.6, MB - MB), "boundary ≈ 23½ yd", (-4.9, (-HALF - MB) / 2))
dim(fld, zh, (-6.6, 0.0), (-6.6, HALF - MB - 0.2), "field ≈ 30 yd", (-4.9, (HALF - MB) / 2 + 4.0))
plt.show()
```

## The deep layer: thirds, halves and quarters

Above the underneath zones the field is split between the deep defenders. There are three
standard splits, and almost every coverage you'll meet uses one of them.

```{python}
#| label: fig-deep-splits
#| fig-cap: "The three ways to split the deep field, with the cornerbacks (CB) and safeties (FS, SS) where they end up after the snap, at their deep landmarks; the underneath defenders are plain squares and the four rushers faint squares at the line. (Before the snap, quarters safeties often stand shallower than this; see the shell section.) Thirds (Cover 3): two corners and one safety, each about 18 yards wide, leaving four underneath. Halves (Cover 2): two safeties, each 27 yards wide, leaving five underneath, with the corners in the flats. Quarters (Cover 4): two corners and two safeties, each about 13 yards wide, leaving three underneath. Bottom right, the trade in one picture: with four rushing, every defender added deep is one taken from underneath."
SPLITS = {
    "Thirds (Cover 3)": dict(edges=[-HALF, -HALF / 3, HALF / 3, HALF], names=["deep ⅓", "deep ⅓", "deep ⅓"],
                             deep=[(18.0, -17.0, "CB"), (18.0, 0.0, "FS"), (18.0, 17.0, "CB")],
                             under=[(7.0, -14.0), (8.5, -5.0), (8.5, 5.0), (7.0, 14.0)]),
    "Halves (Cover 2)": dict(edges=[-HALF, 0.0, HALF], names=["deep ½", "deep ½"],
                             deep=[(18.0, -12.0, "FS"), (18.0, 12.0, "SS")],
                             under=[(5.0, -18.5), (8.5, -9.5), (9.5, 0.0), (8.5, 9.5), (5.0, 18.5)],
                             under_lab={0: "CB", 4: "CB"}),
    "Quarters (Cover 4)": dict(edges=[-HALF, -HALF / 2, 0.0, HALF / 2, HALF], names=["¼", "¼", "¼", "¼"],
                               deep=[(17.0, -19.0, "CB"), (15.5, -6.5, "FS"), (15.5, 6.5, "SS"), (17.0, 19.0, "CB")],
                               under=[(7.0, -12.0), (8.0, 0.0), (7.0, 12.0)]),
}


def split_panel(ax, title, spec):
    p = Play([O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q")], [], los=40, to_go=None)
    fld = Field(ax=ax, orient="vertical", los=40, window=(-3.0, 31.0), numbers=False, lateral=None)
    ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
    e = spec["edges"]
    for i, (a, b) in enumerate(zip(e[:-1], e[1:])):
        zone_box(fld, p, 14.0, 29.5, a + 0.5, b - 0.5, "", alpha=0.10 if i % 2 == 0 else 0.20)
        say(fld, p, 26.5, (a + b) / 2, spec["names"][i], color=style.INK, fontsize=6.6, box=False)
    marks = [(d, w, lab, 1.65) for d, w, lab in spec["deep"]]
    marks += [(d, w, spec.get("under_lab", {}).get(i, ""), 1.4) for i, (d, w) in enumerate(spec["under"])]
    for d, w, lab, rad in marks:
        x, y = P(fld, p, d, w)
        draw_marker(ax, float(x), float(y), "def", "", ppy, r=rad)
        if lab:
            ax.text(float(x), float(y), lab, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=5.6, fontweight="bold",
                    color=style.INK, zorder=10)
    for w in (-6.0, -2.0, 2.0, 6.0):           # four rushers, drawn faint
        x, y = P(fld, p, 1.0, w)
        ax.add_patch(RegularPolygon((float(x), float(y)), 4, radius=0.9, orientation=np.pi / 4, fc="none",
                                    ec=GREY, lw=0.8, zorder=7))
    x, y = P(fld, p, -0.6, 0.0)
    ax.plot([float(x)], [float(y)], marker="o", ms=4, color=style.BALL, zorder=8)
    panel_title(ax, title, fs=8.5)


fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6.6, 5.2))
for ax, (title, spec) in zip(axes.flat, SPLITS.items()):
    split_panel(ax, title, spec)
ax = axes[1, 1]
rows = [("Cover 3", 3, 4), ("Cover 2", 2, 5), ("Cover 4", 4, 3)]
for i, (nm, deep, under) in enumerate(rows):
    y = 2 - i
    ax.barh(y, deep, color=style.DEFENSE, height=0.55)
    ax.barh(y, under, left=deep, color=style.DEFENSE_TINT, edgecolor=style.DEFENSE, lw=0.8, height=0.55)
    ax.text(deep / 2, y, f"{deep} deep", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7.5, color="white", fontweight="bold")
    ax.text(deep + under / 2, y, f"{under} under", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7.5, color=style.INK)
ax.set_yticks([2, 1, 0], [nm for nm, _, _ in rows], fontsize=8)
ax.set_xlim(0, 7.2)
ax.set_xticks([0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7])
ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.set_xlabel("defenders in coverage (four rush)", fontsize=7.5)
panel_title(ax, "The trade: deep vs underneath", fs=8.5)
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.2, w_pad=1.0)
plt.show()
```

- **A [deep third](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-deep-third)** is a third of the field's width,
  about 18 yards. In [Cover 3](06-03-cover-3-family.qmd) the two cornerbacks take the outside
  thirds and a safety the middle one. *What it buys:* only three deep, so four defenders underneath
  and, often, a safety free to come down and help against the run. *What it gives up:* each deep
  defender has a wide strip to himself, and four vertical routes against three deep defenders
  leave one of them guarding two. The seams, the lanes where one third meets the next, are the
  classic targets.
- **A [deep half](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-deep-half)** is half the field's width, about 27
  yards, each guarded by a safety in [Cover 2](06-04-cover-2-and-tampa-2.qmd). *What it buys:* five
  underneath, the most of any zone, so the short and intermediate throws are crowded, and the
  corners can sit in the flats. *What it gives up:* each safety has the widest deep zone there is,
  so a throw down the sideline behind the corner (the "hole shot") or straight up the middle
  between the two safeties stresses him.
- **A [deep quarter](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-deep-quarter)** is a quarter of the width,
  about 13 yards: two corners outside, two safeties inside, in
  [quarters](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cover-4) (Cover 4). *What it buys:* four deep defenders
  each guarding a narrow lane, so deep throws are hard, and because the lanes are narrow the
  safeties can stand closer to the line and jump into the run fit. *What it gives up:* only three
  underneath, so the short areas outside are thin, and a safety who comes up for the run has a
  long way back if it's play-action. One more thing makes quarters different, and it matters later
  in this chapter: the four deep players don't just guard lanes, they read receivers. Each safety
  watches the inside receiver on his side (#2): if #2 runs vertically, the safety covers him like a
  man; if #2 runs short or out, the safety drops off him to help on the outside receiver, or comes
  up to stop the run. Each corner takes the outside receiver (#1) deep wherever he goes, unless #1
  runs a short route. That makes quarters the purest example of the pattern-matching zone described
  below.

These splits are where the first coverage numbers come from: three deep is Cover 3, two deep is
Cover 2, four deep is Cover 4. Hold that thought until the numbering section; first, how a single
defender lines up.

## How a defender lines up: press, off and bail

Now zoom in on one cornerback and one wide receiver. Before the snap the corner has two choices to
make, and each of them sends a message.

```{python}
#| label: fig-press-off-bail
#| fig-cap: "Three ways for a cornerback (CB) to play the same wide receiver (X), drawn on the offense's left. Press: within about a yard, shaded to the outside because his help is in the middle, ready to jam X with his hands. Off: about 8 yards away, also shaded outside; the gap between them is the cushion. Bail, here from a press look: he lines up a yard or two off (dashed outline), then at the snap turns his hips and runs, bending toward a deep-third landmark: the alignment of a man defender and the job of a zone defender. The grey dashed line marks 5 yards past the line of scrimmage: all of the corner's contact has to happen short of it."
def one_on_one(kind):
    p = Play([O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0), O("LT", "LT", -0.7, -3.2, "")],
             [D("LCB", "CB", 1.0, -15.6, "CB")], los=40, to_go=None)
    if kind == "off":
        p.players["LCB"] = p.players["LCB"].moved(d=7.5, w=-16.0)
    if kind == "bail":
        p.players["LCB"] = p.players["LCB"].moved(d=13.0, w=-18.2)
    return p


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(6.6, 3.3))
for ax, kind in zip(axes, ("press", "off", "bail")):
    p = one_on_one(kind)
    p.highlight("LCB")
    fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=(-25.0, -5.5), window=(-3.5, 18.0), title=False)
    clean(ax)
    ruler(fld, p, fs=5.5)
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = P(fld, p, 5.0, -25.0), P(fld, p, 5.0, -5.5)
    ax.plot([float(x0), float(x1)], [float(y0), float(y1)], color=style.INK_2, lw=1.1, ls=(0, (4, 2)),
            zorder=2)
    if kind == "press":
        say(fld, p, 6.9, -10.0, "5 yd: contact\nends here", fontsize=6.0, color=style.INK_2)
        say(fld, p, 2.5, -9.6, "within a yard,\nhands on him\nat the snap", fontsize=6.3)
        say(fld, p, 10.5, -15.0, "eyes: the receiver\n(man), or a peek\nat the QB (zone)", fontsize=6.3)
        panel_title(ax, "Press", fs=8.5)
    elif kind == "off":
        dim(fld, p, (0.1, -18.5), (7.3, -18.5), "", (3.6, -18.5))
        say(fld, p, 3.6, -21.3, "cushion\n≈ 8 yd", fontsize=6.3)
        say(fld, p, 11.5, -13.0, "outside shade,\nturned in to see\nthe quarterback", fontsize=6.3)
        panel_title(ax, "Off", fs=8.5)
    else:
        ghost(fld, p, 1.6, -15.8, "CB")
        path(fld, p, [(2.3, -16.0), (7.0, -16.9), (12.2, -18.0)])
        say(fld, p, 8.5, -11.2, "looks like press,\nturns and runs\nat the snap", fontsize=6.3)
        panel_title(ax, "Bail (from a press look)", fs=8.5)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8)
plt.show()
```

**How close?** In **[press](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-press)** the defender lines up within
about a yard of the receiver and tries to jam him with his hands at the snap: punch his chest,
turn his shoulders, push him off the line he wants to run. A route is a timing play
([The Quick Game](../04-the-passing-game/04-03-quick-game.qmd)): the quarterback's feet tell him
when to throw, and a slant that should break after three steps but breaks after five because the
receiver was wrestling at the line arrives after the quarterback has had to move on. *What press
buys:* the defender is right there, so short throws are contested and the timing is wrecked.
*What it gives up:* if the receiver beats the jam with a quick move, the defender is beaten at the
line with nothing but grass ahead of the receiver, so press almost always comes with help deep.

In **[off coverage](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-off-coverage)** the defender starts several
yards away, usually 5 to 10, and gives ground at the snap. The gap between them is the
**[cushion](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cushion)**: how many yards of depth the defender has
on the receiver. Cushion is time. A receiver needs a second or more to eat up eight yards, and
in that second the defender reads the route and the quarterback. *What off coverage buys:* it's
very hard to get behind a defender who starts eight yards deep and keeps backing up. *What it
gives up:* the receiver can stop in front of him (a hitch, a quick out) and catch the ball before
the defender can close the gap. When the analyst says "he's giving a big cushion," he means the
defense has decided it would rather give up five yards than fifty. Many coaches teach the cushion
as a budget: backpedal while it lasts, and when the receiver has eaten it down to two or three
yards, stop giving ground, turn and run with him, or drive on him if he stops.

**Which side?** The defender's alignment also has a lean, its
[leverage](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-leverage-inside-outside): shaded inside the receiver, he
is protecting the middle of the field and daring the receiver to go outside, toward the sideline
(which acts like an extra defender); shaded outside, he's protecting the sideline and pushing the
receiver inside, usually because he knows he has help in the middle. Leverage is never random. It
tells you where the defender's help is, which is why quarterbacks are taught to throw away from it.

The third option is a technique, and sometimes a lie. To
**[bail](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-bail)**, a corner turns his hips at the snap and runs to a
deep landmark instead of backpedalling. From an off alignment it is an everyday technique, the
usual way a Cover 3 corner gets to his deep third against a fast receiver, because nobody can
backpedal as fast as a receiver can sprint. From a press look, a yard or two off, it becomes a
disguise, often called *press-bail*. Why line up close only to leave? Because a pressed corner says
"man coverage" to the quarterback, and the quarterback reacts: he expects his receiver to run away
from a defender who has his back turned, and he expects quick throws to beat press. If the corner
bails into a deep third instead, the quarterback is throwing at a zone he thought was man.
Press-bail is the cheapest disguise in football, and it costs something too: a corner who starts at
two yards and has to reach eighteen is running backward and sideways while the receiver runs
forward, so the deep ball outside is a risk. The full art of
showing one thing and playing another is the subject of
[Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage](06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd).

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"The corner who lines up close is playing man; the one who backs off is playing zone." It's a
lean, not a rule. The classic Cover 2 corner is often right up on the receiver: a
[hard corner](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hard-corner) who jams #1, knocks him off his line
toward the safety, and then sinks into the flat, a zone player in a press alignment. Seattle's
famous Cover 3 corners pressed receivers and then ran with them into their deep thirds (film room,
below). And plenty of man-coverage corners play off on third-and-long, because the first job of any
coverage on third-and-12 is to keep the receiver from getting past the sticks *and* past the
defender. Read the corner's alignment together with his eyes and the safeties,
never alone.
:::

### Trail, and the defender's eyes

Once the ball is snapped, a man defender has to decide where to be relative to his receiver.
The most common choice, when there's a safety deep to help, is
**[trail technique](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-trail-technique)**: run a step behind the
receiver and slightly underneath him, on his hip. Why behind? Because the defender has handed the
deep ball over the top to the safety, so his job is the throws *in front of* the receiver: the
slant, the dig, the out. From the hip he can drive on any break and get a hand on the ball. The
price is the deep ball if the help never arrives, and the back-shoulder throw, aimed at the
receiver's back hip, where the trailing defender can't reach.
([Man Coverage](06-02-man-coverage.qmd) builds the other man techniques.)

```{python}
#| label: fig-trail
#| fig-cap: "Trail, and what \"underneath\" means. Left: with a free safety deep, the corner runs a step behind X and on his inside hip, between X and the quarterback, so the short and in-breaking throws (shaded) have to go through him; the deep ball is the safety's. Right, for contrast: with no help behind him, a man defender stays level with or deeper than the receiver (on top), and the short throw in front of him is the price."
def trail_panel(ax, kind):
    XP = (12.5, -15.8)
    p = Play([O("X", "WR", *XP)], [], los=40, to_go=None)
    fld = Field(ax=ax, orient="vertical", los=40, window=(-2.5, 23.0), numbers=False,
                lateral=sorted((p.ball_y + 24.5, p.ball_y + 2.0)), to_go=None)
    ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
    xs, ys = P(fld, p, np.array([-0.7, 11.6]), np.array([-15.8, -15.8]))
    ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.8, zorder=4)
    ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((xs[0], ys[0]), (xs[1], ys[1]), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=9,
                                 color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.6, zorder=4))
    if kind == "trail":
        zone_box(fld, p, 4.0, 9.5, -12.8, -5.2, "", alpha=0.18)
        say(fld, p, 6.8, -9.0, "his throws:\nslant, dig, out", fontsize=6.2)
        cb = (10.6, -13.6)
        path(fld, p, [(1.0, -15.2), (6.0, -14.2), (9.6, -13.7)])
        say(fld, p, 15.6, -10.8, "a step behind,\non his inside hip", fontsize=6.2)
        fs = (19.5, -6.0)
        x, y = P(fld, p, *fs)
        draw_marker(ax, float(x), float(y), "def", "FS", ppy)
        path(fld, p, [(19.5, -7.2), (19.0, -12.0)], lw=1.1)
        say(fld, p, 21.0, -13.0, "deep ball: the safety's", fontsize=6.2)
        panel_title(ax, "Trail (help deep)", fs=8.2)
    else:
        zone_box(fld, p, 2.0, 9.5, -12.8, -5.2, "", alpha=0.10)
        say(fld, p, 5.8, -9.0, "his price:\nthe short throw", fontsize=6.2)
        cb = (14.4, -13.9)
        path(fld, p, [(7.0, -14.4), (10.5, -14.0), (13.4, -13.9)])
        say(fld, p, 17.8, -14.5, "level or deeper:\nnothing behind him", fontsize=6.2)
        say(fld, p, 21.0, -7.0, "no safety", fontsize=6.2, color=GREY)
        panel_title(ax, "On top (no help)", fs=8.2)
    for (d, w), lab, side in ((cb, "CB", "def"), (XP, "X", "off")):
        x, y = P(fld, p, d, w)
        draw_marker(ax, float(x), float(y), side, lab, ppy, ring=style.THIRD if lab == "CB" else None)
    x, y = P(fld, p, -0.6, -3.0)
    ax.plot([float(x)], [float(y)], marker="o", ms=0)
    ruler(fld, p, fs=5.5, top=20)


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.0, 3.0))
for ax, kind in zip(axes, ("trail", "top")):
    trail_panel(ax, kind)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.0)
plt.show()
```

Which brings us to the most underrated skill in coverage, **[eye discipline](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-eye-discipline)**:
looking at the right thing at the right moment. A man defender looks at his man, mostly at his
hips, which can't fake where the receiver is going the way a head or shoulders can. A zone defender
looks at the quarterback, because the quarterback's eyes and shoulders tell him where the ball is
going, and he "feels" the receivers entering his area out of the corner of his eye. The two have
opposite failure modes. A man defender who peeks at the quarterback loses a step on his receiver.
A zone defender who stares at a receiver drifts with him, out of his zone, and the window he was
supposed to close opens behind him; one who stares at the quarterback can be moved by a
[play-action](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-play-action) fake or a quarterback who looks one
way and throws the other. Coaches call a defender caught looking at the wrong thing an *eye
violation*, and when you see a receiver running wide open on a replay, the first question to ask
is where the nearest defender was looking.

### The 5-yard rule

Press has a legal limit, and it shapes the whole position. In the NFL a defender may make contact
with a receiver only until the receiver is 5 yards past the line of scrimmage. After that,
until the ball is thrown, and as long as the quarterback is still in the pocket with it, any
contact that impedes him (beyond incidental contact) is
[illegal contact](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-illegal-contact), a 5-yard penalty with an
automatic first down, and grabbing him is [defensive holding](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-defensive-holding),
the same penalty.[^contactrule]

It wasn't always so. For most of the league's history a defender could keep hitting a receiver
downfield until the ball was thrown, and physical cornerbacks such as the Steelers' Mel Blount
turned every route into a fight. The league trimmed that in steps through the 1970s: in 1977
defenders were allowed to contact a receiver only once,[^chuck1977] and in 1978 the rule that
still applies limited contact to the first 5 yards, a change still called the
"Mel Blount rule."[^blount] The league tightened it again after the January 2004 AFC Championship
Game, in which New England's corners, led by Ty Law, manhandled Indianapolis's receivers: from 2004
officials were told to enforce illegal contact and pass interference strictly, a crackdown many
called the "Ty Law rule."[^tylaw] Both changes made passing easier, and both are part of why
passing numbers have climbed for decades ([The 1978 Liberation](../11-history/11-02-the-1978-liberation.qmd)).

Why does this matter for reading coverage? Because it explains why press lives where it lives.
Inside 5 yards the corner may jam, re-jam and ride the receiver; past 5 yards he may not touch him
at all. All of the contact has to happen in those first 5 yards, about the first second of the
route, so press is about the release, and a receiver who gets through it clean is in open space
with a defender chasing him. It's why pressed corners nearly always
have a safety behind them, why offenses love quick, sharp releases and stacked receivers against
press (one receiver behind another, so the defender can't get his hands on the back one), and
why on third-and-long, when the receiver will run well past 5 yards, many defenses don't bother to
press at all. [Contact Rules and Penalties as Strategy](../09-special-teams-and-the-rules-that-shape-strategy/09-03-contact-rules-and-penalties.qmd)
covers the rule book side, including pass interference.

## Three ways to guard a receiver: spot-drop, pattern-match and man

You've met man and zone. In the modern NFL, zone itself comes in two styles, and the difference
between them is most of the story of coverage since the 1990s.

In **[spot-drop zone](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-spot-drop-zone)** each defender drops to his
landmark and then plays the quarterback: when the quarterback looks, he leans; when the ball is
thrown, he breaks on it. He guards an area, whoever comes through it. In
**[pattern matching](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pattern-matching)** each defender starts as a
zone player but reads the receivers' routes as they develop, and by rule (an if-then rule agreed
before the play) picks up whoever enters or stays in his area and covers him like man, passing him
off to a teammate if he leaves. "If #2 goes to the flat, I take him; if he goes vertical, I carry
him up the seam," where *carry* means stay with him as he runs deeper. A match zone is a zone
coverage that turns into man coverage once the routes declare (once each receiver has shown where
he's going, usually in the first second or so), so that each receiver has a defender on him
wherever the offense put him. Quarters, with its safeties reading #2, is the classic example.

The easiest way to see the three is to run the same routes against all of them.

```{python}
#| label: fig-three-ways
#| fig-cap: "The same two routes against three kinds of coverage (offense's left side; simulated play). X runs a dig (up to 12 yards, then across); H runs a short out, so the routes cross. All three rows start from the same alignment; watch the ringed nickel ($) and Will (W). At +0.6 s the man $ is already moving with H, while the two zone $s are still dropping. Spot-drop (top): the $ sinks to his curl landmark and leaves H to run under him into the flat; the dig settles in the window between the $ and the W, who break on the throw too late. Pattern-match (middle): the $ picks up H when he breaks out, the W picks up the dig, and the CB carries X, hands him off and stays deep: nobody is open. Man (bottom): the CB and $ chase their men with their backs to the quarterback (the CB undercutting the dig from X's inside hip), and the W, with no receiver, sits in the hole as a rat. On the web this is a video."
LAT, WIN = (-21.0, 2.5), (-9.0, 19.5)
THROW_T = 1.6


def catch_time(p, t_throw):
    """When the thrown ball reaches its target (same flight model as gridiron)."""
    start = p.ball_position(t_throw)
    t_arr = t_throw + 0.5
    for _ in range(5):
        t_arr = t_throw + float(np.linalg.norm(p.position("X", t_arr) - start)) / gplay.BALL_SPEED
    return t_arr


def break_on_ball(p, key, landmark, t_land, t_react, t_arr, stop=3.0):
    """Zone drop to a landmark, sit, then break toward the catch point after the throw, arriving late."""
    q = p.players[key]
    catch = p.position("X", t_arr)
    lm = np.array(landmark)
    v = catch - lm
    dist = float(np.linalg.norm(v))
    end = lm + v * max(0.0, (dist - stop) / dist)
    rows = [(t_land, *lm), (t_react, *lm), (t_arr, *end), (t_arr + 0.6, *end)]
    set_track(p, key, rows)


def three_ways(kind):
    off = line5()[:3] + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -1.5, "R"),
                         O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0), O("H", "WR", -1.5, -9.0)]
    dfn = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -5.6, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.8, "T"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -3.0, "W"),
           D("NB", "NB", 5.0, -7.6, "$"), D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -16.0, "CB"), D("FS", "FS", 13.0, 0.0, "FS")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=None)
    p.route("X", r.dig(12.0, 6.0))
    p.route("H", r.out(5.0, 7.5))
    p.dropback(2.5)
    p.block("RB", pts=[(0.6, -1.4)])
    protect(p, rushers=("WDE", "WDT"), linemen=("LT", "LG", "C"))
    if kind == "spot":
        p.drop("LCB", (17.5, -16.5), speed=4.6)
        p.drop("FS", (17.0, -1.0), speed=3.5)
        p.pass_to("X", t=THROW_T)
        t_arr = catch_time(p, THROW_T)
        break_on_ball(p, "NB", (10.5, -15.0), 1.7, THROW_T + 0.4, t_arr, stop=3.5)
        break_on_ball(p, "WILL", (10.0, -2.8), 1.4, THROW_T + 0.4, t_arr, stop=3.5)
    elif kind == "match":
        p.drop("FS", (16.5, -2.5), speed=3.5)
        set_track(p, "NB", [(0.6, 6.8, -9.8)] + shadow(p, "NB", "H", off=(1.2, 1.7), lag=0.25, t_from=0.6,
                                                        t_on=1.3, start=(6.8, -9.8)))
        set_track(p, "LCB", [(1.3, 11.0, -15.9), (2.0, 13.8, -14.8), (3.0, 16.0, -14.0)])
        set_track(p, "WILL", [(0.9, 7.5, -4.4), (1.6, 9.2, -6.0), (2.4, 9.4, -7.4), (3.0, 9.4, -7.4)])
    else:
        p.drop("FS", (17.0, -1.0), speed=3.5)
        p.drop("WILL", (7.5, -2.0), speed=2.5)
        # hand-keyed man play: the CB backpedals, then undercuts the dig from X's inside hip;
        # the $ mirrors H, holding his cushion, then drives on the out
        set_track(p, "LCB", [(0.6, 7.6, -15.9), (1.2, 9.4, -15.6), (1.6, 10.4, -15.0), (2.0, 9.8, -12.8),
                             (2.4, 9.7, -9.8), (3.0, 9.7, -9.6)])
        set_track(p, "NB", [(0.6, 5.5, -8.7), (0.9, 5.3, -9.6), (1.3, 4.9, -12.6), (1.7, 4.9, -14.8),
                            (2.4, 4.9, -15.0), (3.0, 4.9, -15.0)])
    return p


THREE = [("Spot-drop", three_ways("spot"), THROW_T), ("Pattern-match", three_ways("match"), None),
         ("Man", three_ways("man"), None)]
TIMES = [0.0, 0.6, 1.2, 2.4]
RINGS = ("NB", "WILL")
EARLY = {"Spot-drop": "$ drops\nto a spot", "Pattern-match": "$ drops:\nzone so far",
         "Man": "$ goes with\nH at once"}
FINAL = {"Spot-drop": "$ sank to the curl, H ran\nunder him; the dig settles\nbetween $ and W",
         "Pattern-match": "$ took the out, W the dig;\nCB carried X, handed him\noff and stayed deep",
         "Man": "CB and $ chase their men,\nbacks to the QB. W has\nno man: rat in the hole"}

if PDF:
    span_w, span_d = abs(LAT[1] - LAT[0]), WIN[1] - WIN[0]
    pw = 6.4 / 4
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 4, figsize=(6.4, 3 * (pw * span_d / span_w + 0.26)))
    for row, (name, p, tt) in enumerate(THREE):
        for col, t in enumerate(TIMES):
            fld = moment(axes[row, col], p, t, LAT, WIN, rings=RINGS, throw_t=tt)
            lab = "snap" if t == 0 else f"+{t:.1f} s"
            panel_title(axes[row, col], f"{name} · {lab}", fs=6.8)
            if col == 1:
                tag(fld, p, t, EARLY[name], fs=5.6)
            if col == 3:
                tag(fld, p, t, FINAL[name], fs=5.4)
    fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.6, w_pad=0.3)
    plt.show()
else:
    from matplotlib import animation
    from IPython.display import HTML, display
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(7.4, 3.6))
    ts = np.round(np.arange(-0.3, 2.81, 0.1), 2)

    def update(i):
        for ax, (name, p, tt) in zip(axes, THREE):
            ax.clear()
            t = max(0.0, float(ts[i]))
            fld = moment(ax, p, t, LAT, WIN, rings=RINGS, throw_t=tt)
            panel_title(ax, f"{name} · " + ("snap" if t == 0 else f"+{t:.1f} s"), fs=9)
            if 0.5 <= t <= 1.0:
                tag(fld, p, t, EARLY[name], fs=6.5)
            if t >= 2.3:
                tag(fld, p, t, FINAL[name], fs=6.0)
        return []

    fig.tight_layout()
    anim = animation.FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=len(ts), interval=100)
    html = (anim.to_html5_video(embed_limit=40).replace("<video ", '<video style="max-width:100%;height:auto" ')
            if shutil.which("ffmpeg") else anim.to_jshtml(default_mode="once"))
    plt.close(fig)
    display(HTML(html))
```

Watch one defender in each row, the nickel ($), for the first second. In man he goes with H from
the first step: at +0.6 s he is already shuffling outside with him, holding his cushion, eyes on
H. In spot-drop and pattern-match he looks the same at +0.6 s: he turns and drops toward the curl
like a zone player, eyes on the quarterback. The two zones split when H breaks out, just under a
second in. The pattern-match $ sees #2 go to the flat and comes down with him; the spot-drop $
keeps sinking to his curl landmark and lets H run underneath him, because his job is a place, and
he trusts that a throw to the flat is short and he can break on it. **That first second is how you
tell them apart on a replay:** did the defender run *to a spot* or *with a receiver*, and if with a
receiver, did he start with him or pick him up after a beat?

Then look at the Will (W) in each row. In spot-drop he sits in his hook zone and the dig settles in
the window between him and the $. In pattern-match he picks up the dig as it crosses into his area.
In man he has no receiver at all (the running back stayed in to block), so he becomes an extra
defender sitting in the hole, which is why man coverage defenses so often have a "free" player.

Now the trade-offs, which are the reason all three still exist.

- **Spot-drop zone** is simple to teach, keeps every defender's eyes on the quarterback, and gives
  the offense nothing deep: it's hard to complete a long pass over defenders who are dropping to
  depth and reading the throw. But it is passive. The windows between the landmarks are a known
  size, and an offense that runs receivers into those windows, or puts two receivers into one
  defender's area (the [flood](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-flood) concept is built to do
  exactly that), completes balls all day. The top row shows the classic case: a dig that settles
  between two defenders who both did their jobs. The trade is that both of them are facing the
  ball when it's thrown, so they break on it together and the catch gains what it gains and no
  more.
- **Pattern matching** fixes that by letting the routes decide who covers whom. Each receiver ends
  up with a defender on him, but the defenders started as zone players, facing the quarterback, so
  they still see scrambles and throws coming. The price is complexity. Every defender needs rules
  for every combination of routes ("#2 out, I take the flat; #2 vertical, I carry him; #1 under, I
  pass him to the hook"), the rules have to agree with each other, and a defender who misreads one
  route can leave two defenders on one receiver and none on another. Offenses fight match with
  routes that change direction late, crossing routes that force defenders to pass receivers off to
  each other at full speed, and motion before the snap.
- **Man coverage** is the tightest of all: every receiver has a shadow from the first step. It's
  also the most fragile. Defenders have their backs to the quarterback (so a scramble is dangerous;
  look at the bottom row), crossing routes and rubs make them run through traffic, and one lost
  footrace means a big play. [Man Coverage](06-02-man-coverage.qmd) covers when defenses choose it
  anyway.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists: pattern matching"}
**The problem it solved.** Spot-drop zones were the standard for decades, and by the 1980s and
1990s offenses had learned to beat them by design: four receivers running vertically against three
deep defenders, or two receivers flooding one curl-flat defender. The answer was to make the zone
react to the routes. Nick Saban, building a pattern-matching Cover 3 with Bill Belichick in
Cleveland in the early 1990s, is the coach most often credited, and his later Michigan State, LSU
and Alabama defenses spread the idea through college football; the coaching writer Cameron
Soran, whose guide to Saban's coverages is the most detailed public account, writes that this kind of Cover 3 "simply did not exist" before then.[^saban] Like most "who
invented it" stories, it's disputed: zone defenders have always adjusted to routes somewhat, and
other staffs developed match rules in parallel. Today almost every NFL zone matches to some degree,
which is why the man/zone labels in charting data are fuzzier than they look.

**What it gives up.** Teaching time, and certainty. A match coverage has dozens of rules, and
offenses design plays specifically to make two defenders' rules contradict each other.
:::

## Reading the shell: is the middle of the field closed or open?

[A First Look at Defense](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd) taught
the two shells, one-high and two-high, and the corner tell that goes with them. It also named the
coaches' words for them, which this chapter now makes official:

- **[MOFC](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-mofc)**, the
  [middle of the field closed](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-middle-of-field-closed): one deep
  safety in the middle of the field, so the deep middle is guarded. That's a one-high defense: Cover
  1 (man underneath) or Cover 3 (zone underneath), most of the time.
- **[MOFO](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-mofo)**, the
  [middle of the field open](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-middle-of-field-open): nobody in the
  deep middle, usually because two safeties have split the field between them. That's two-high:
  Cover 2, quarters, 2-Man (Cover 2's two deep safeties with man coverage underneath) or Cover 6
  (quarters on one side, Cover 2 on the other; more on both numbers below). Cover 0, with no safety
  deep at all, also counts as "open": the label answers the quarterback's question "is anyone
  guarding the deep middle?", and in Cover 0 nobody is.

Why talk about the *middle* rather than counting safeties? Because the deep middle is the most
dangerous place on the field to leave unguarded. A ball thrown down the middle can be caught with
room to run either way, and the post route (a deep route breaking toward the goalposts) is the
easiest deep throw for a quarterback to make, straight ahead with no sideline to squeeze it. That
is why coaches call the deep middle itself "the post", and a lone safety there the post safety. So
the quarterback's first question after "how many deep?" is really "is anyone in the post?" It
decides his best deep throw: against MOFC, attack outside, down the sidelines and up the seams
beside the deep safety; against MOFO, attack the middle, between the safeties.

It also feeds the *option routes* that
[Passing Fundamentals](../04-the-passing-game/04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd) introduced. The core
rule there was about the underneath defenders: against man, break away from your defender; against
zone, find the soft spot between two defenders and sit. The shell is a fast first guess at that,
because MOFC with defenders tight on the receivers usually means Cover 1, man, and so "break away";
two-high usually means a zone, and so "sit". But the guess has exceptions the receiver has to
read through: Cover 3 is MOFC and a zone (sit in the window), and 2-Man is MOFO with every
underneath defender in trail man (break away). For a receiver running *deep*, the shell gives its
own rule: against MOFC, bend away from the post safety (toward the sideline or up the seam);
against MOFO, split the two safeties or take the post.

### Depth and width: what the safeties and corners tell you

Inside each family, the details of the alignment narrow it down, because every defender lines up
where his real job is reachable. Here are four common pictures against the same offense.

```{python}
#| label: fig-shells
#| fig-cap: "Four pre-snap pictures against the same 2x2 offense, safeties and corners ringed. Top row, both middle of the field closed: compare the corners (pressed and square, with every receiver covered tight, against 7 to 8 yards off with the slot defenders inside). Bottom row, both middle of the field open: compare the safeties' depth and width (deeper and wider for Cover 2, shallower and tighter to the hash for quarters). In both two-high pictures a linebacker stands in the apex outside the right tackle, over the slot tight end. Each picture is a lean, not a guarantee."
MOFO_LB = dict(MIKE=(4.8, 5.6), WILL=(4.5, -0.8))   # apex over Y, and a linebacker stacked over the ball
SHELLS = {
    "MOFC · pressed, everyone on a man (Cover 1 look)": dict(
        FS=(14.0, 0.0), SS=(4.0, 8.4), NB=(1.6, -8.4), LCB=(1.3, -15.7), RCB=(1.3, 15.7), MIKE=(4.5, 1.2),
        WILL=(4.5, -2.4)),
    "MOFC · off, eyes in (Cover 3 look)": dict(
        FS=(14.0, 0.0), SS=(5.5, 6.9), NB=(5.0, -6.9), LCB=(7.5, -16.3), RCB=(7.5, 16.3)),
    "MOFO · deep and wide, corners squat (Cover 2 look)": dict(
        FS=(13.0, -7.5), SS=(13.0, 7.5), NB=(4.5, -6.8), LCB=(5.0, -16.4), RCB=(5.0, 16.4), **MOFO_LB),
    "MOFO · shallow and tight (quarters look)": dict(
        FS=(10.0, -4.5), SS=(10.0, 4.5), NB=(4.5, -6.8), LCB=(7.5, -15.8), RCB=(7.5, 15.8), **MOFO_LB),
}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.6))
for ax, (title, spots) in zip(axes.flat, SHELLS.items()):
    p = Play(spread(), nickel(**spots), los=40, to_go=None)
    p.highlight("FS", "SS", "LCB", "RCB")
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-21.5, 21.5), window=(-6.5, 19.5), rfs=5.0)
    fs = spots["FS"]
    if fs[1] == 0.0:
        say(fld, p, fs[0] + 2.4, 0.0, f"{fs[0]:.0f} yd deep, in the middle", fontsize=5.6)
    else:
        wtxt = f"{abs(fs[1]):.1f}".replace(".5", "½").replace(".0", "")
        say(fld, p, fs[0] + 2.9, 0.0, f"both {fs[0]:.0f} yd deep,\n{wtxt} yd from the middle", fontsize=5.6)
    panel_title(ax, title, fs=7.4)
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.9, w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

The tells, and the reason behind each:

- **Safety depth.** Two-high safeties in Cover 2 line up deep, 12 to 14 yards, because each is
  responsible for the deepest ball thrown anywhere in his half of the field. Quarters safeties
  can line up shallower, 8 to 11 yards, because their deep zone is narrow and they are also run
  defenders: they read the slot receiver or tight end in front of them, and if it's a run, they
  fly downhill. A single high safety in Cover 3 or Cover 1 is usually the deepest player on the
  field, 13 to 16 yards. **In the NFL, treat depth as a weak tell.** Many two-high defenses,
  Fangio's and the many copied from it, line every safety up at the same 12 to 14 yards whatever
  the call, precisely so that depth won't give the coverage away; the shallow quarters safety is
  more of a college picture.
- **Safety width.** A Cover 2 safety has half the field, so he lines up wider, several yards
  outside the hash and closer to the slot receiver, to be able to reach the sideline. A quarters
  safety has only the inside quarter and reads the slot receiver, so he lines up tighter, nearer
  the hash and well inside that receiver. On the NFL's narrow hashes the difference is only a few
  yards, so compare the safety with the slot receiver on his side: closer to the slot leans halves,
  closer to the hash leans quarters. Width that doesn't fit the coverage the shell suggests (a
  "two-high" safety who is almost in the middle) is a classic rotation tell
  ([Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage](06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd)).
- **Corner depth and leverage.** Cover 2 corners have the flat, so they play short: squatting at
  about 5 yards, or pressing to jam #1 and knock him inside before sinking to the flat, always with
  outside leverage, forcing everything inside to the safety. Cover 3 corners sit 7 to 8 yards off
  with outside leverage and turn their shoulders in to see the quarterback, because they have a
  deep third. Cover 1 corners often press, square to their man, eyes on him, shading toward the
  side away from their help. Quarters corners sit off, eyes on #1, because in quarters they usually
  take #1 deep wherever he goes. That last difference is also the best way to tell Cover 3 from
  quarters *after* the snap, when both showed off corners: the Cover 3 corner turns and bails to a
  landmark, the quarters corner pedals and reads #1.
- **The slot defenders.** A nickel or safety tight on a slot receiver, nose to nose, suggests man;
  one standing a few yards inside him, in the [apex](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-apex) between
  the slot and the tackle, suggests zone.

None of these is a guarantee on its own. The skill is adding them up, and then, as the
quarterback does, checking the answer one second after the snap. The shell before the snap is a
hypothesis; what the safeties do at the snap is the evidence. (Who decides the call, and how it
can change once the defense sees the formation, is in the Madden box below.)

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists: reading the shell"}
**For the quarterback**, the shell is the first filter on the play: it tells him which side and
which receiver to start with, whether the deep ball is outside or in the middle, and whether to
change the play at the line. **For the defense**, the shell is the price of physics: a safety can
only cover so much ground after the snap, so where he stands limits what he can do. That's why the
shell carries real information, and why a defense that wants to lie has to do it carefully, with
safeties who move late or rotate at the snap; the Fangio film room below is the famous example of
a shell that lies on purpose. How often does the pre-snap shell match the coverage played? No
public source we trust gives a league-wide rate. The numbers you'll see count coverages *played*:
Next Gen Stats' split-safety rate, the share of plays in two-high coverages such as Cover 2, 4 and
6, rose from 32.9 percent in 2018 to 42.0 percent in 2025, the highest since its tracking
began.[^ngs]
:::

## Decoding the numbers: Cover 0 to Cover 9

On a broadcast you'll hear coverages called by number: "that's Cover 1," "they're playing a lot of
Cover 6." **[Coverage numbering](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-coverage-numbering-cover-0-9)**
(Cover 0 to Cover 9) is the closest thing football has to a common language for pass defense, and
it starts out simple: **through Cover 4, the number counts the deep defenders.** [Cover 0](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cover-0) has none,
[Cover 1](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cover-1) has one, [Cover 2](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cover-2) has two, [Cover 3](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cover-3) three, [Cover 4](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cover-4) four.

After 4 the counting stops and the numbers become names. Cover 5 isn't five deep (nobody plays
five deep); in most systems it's another name for [2-Man](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cover-5),
two deep with man underneath. [Cover 6](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cover-6) is the most famous non-count: a [split-field coverage](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-split-field-coverage) that
plays quarters on one side and Cover 2 on the other, a quarter, a quarter and a half, and many
coaches remember the number by adding them up: four plus two. Which side gets which matters, and it
is decided by the offense's strength. You met
[formation strength](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-formation-strength) in
[Formation Rules and Vocabulary](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd);
for coverage, the version that usually counts is the *passing strength*, the side with more
receivers. The usual Cover 6 puts its quarters half toward the strength (or the wide field side),
where the receivers are, and its Cover 2 half toward the weak side or the short boundary. From 7 up,
the numbers belong to individual staffs, and you can't decode them without knowing whose playbook
you're in.

```{python}
#| label: fig-dialects
#| fig-cap: "Cover 0 to Cover 9 at a glance: the deep split (shaded, with the share of the width each deep defender guards) and how the underneath players cover: man (blue), zone (orange) or match (purple, zone that turns into man by rule). In the Cover 6 and Cover 8 panels the blue dots are the receivers: three on the left make that the offense's passing strength, and the two coverages are the same idea with the halves swapped. Through Cover 4 the number counts the deep defenders. From Cover 5 on the numbers are names; panels with a dashed border are dialect numbers, drawn in one common meaning (named below each panel), and mean something else in other playbooks. The full dialect table is in Appendix D, the Coverage and Pressure Atlas."
DIAL = [
    ("Cover 0", [], "man", "no deep safety;\nman, usually a blitz", False),
    ("Cover 1", [(-HALF, HALF, "1 free")], "man", "one free safety;\nman underneath", False),
    ("Cover 2", [(-HALF, 0, "½"), (0, HALF, "½")], "zone", "two deep halves;\nfive under", False),
    ("Cover 3", [(-HALF, -HALF / 3, "⅓"), (-HALF / 3, HALF / 3, "⅓"), (HALF / 3, HALF, "⅓")], "zone",
     "three deep thirds;\nfour under", False),
    ("Cover 4", [(-HALF, -HALF / 2, "¼"), (-HALF / 2, 0, "¼"), (0, HALF / 2, "¼"), (HALF / 2, HALF, "¼")],
     "zone", "quarters: four deep,\nthree under", False),
    ("Cover 5", [(-HALF, 0, "½"), (0, HALF, "½")], "man", "usually 2-Man: two\ndeep, man under", True),
    ("Cover 6", [(-HALF, -HALF / 2, "¼"), (-HALF / 2, 0, "¼"), (0, HALF, "½")], "zone",
     "quarters to the 3-receiver\nside, half away", True),
    ("Cover 7", [(-HALF, -HALF / 2, "¼"), (-HALF / 2, 0, "¼"), (0, HALF / 2, "¼"), (HALF / 2, HALF, "¼")],
```
