```{python}
     "match", "Saban: split-field\nmatch, quarters-based", True),
    ("Cover 8", [(-HALF, 0, "½"), (0, HALF / 2, "¼"), (HALF / 2, HALF, "¼")], "zone",
     "Fangio: half to the 3-\nreceiver side, ¼s away", True),
    ("Cover 9", [(-HALF, -HALF / 3, "⅓"), (-HALF / 3, HALF / 3, "⅓"), (HALF / 3, HALF, "⅓")], "match",
     "drawn: Cover 3 match;\nvaries by staff", True),
]


def dial_panel(ax, name, deep, under, note, dialect):
    p = Play([O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q")], [], los=40, to_go=None)
    fld = Field(ax=ax, orient="vertical", los=40, window=(-2.0, 30.0), numbers=False, hashes=False,
                lateral=None)
    for i, (a, b, lab) in enumerate(deep):
        zone_box(fld, p, 15.0, 28.0, a + 0.8, b - 0.8, "", alpha=0.12 if i % 2 == 0 else 0.24, ls="-")
        say(fld, p, 21.5, (a + b) / 2, lab, color=style.INK, fontsize=6.6, box=False, weight="bold")
    if not deep:
        say(fld, p, 21.5, 0.0, "nobody deep", color=DD, fontsize=6.2, box=False)
    col = {"man": style.OFFENSE_DARK, "zone": DD, "match": "#6a4fb0"}[under]
    zone_box(fld, p, 2.0, 12.0, -24.5, 24.5, "", color=col, alpha=0.10, ls="-")
    say(fld, p, 7.0, 0.0, {"man": "man under", "zone": "zone under", "match": "match under"}[under],
        color=col, fontsize=6.4, box=False, weight="bold")
    if name in ("Cover 6", "Cover 8"):         # receivers at the line: three to the offense's left (the strength)
        for w in (-21.0, -14.5, -8.0, 20.0):
            x, y = P(fld, p, -0.9, w)
            ax.plot([float(x)], [float(y)], marker="o", ms=3.2, color=style.OFFENSE, mec="white", mew=0.4,
                    zorder=9)
    if dialect:
        for s in ax.spines.values():
            s.set_visible(True)
        ax.axis("on")
        ax.set_xticks([])
        ax.set_yticks([])
        for s in ax.spines.values():
            s.set_linestyle((0, (3, 2)))
            s.set_edgecolor(style.INK_2)
            s.set_linewidth(0.9)
    ax.set_title(name, fontsize=8.5, color=style.INK, fontweight="bold", loc="center", pad=3)
    ax.text(0.5, -0.06, note, transform=ax.transAxes, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=6.3, color=style.INK_2,
            linespacing=1.15)


fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 5, figsize=(6.6, 3.0))
for ax, args in zip(axes.flat, DIAL):
    dial_panel(ax, *args)
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=2.0, w_pad=0.5)
plt.show()
```

The higher numbers are where football's dialects live. These are real examples, and they are
exactly why the [Coverage and Pressure Atlas](../../appendices/appendix-d-coverage-pressure-atlas.qmd)
keeps a dialect table:

- **Cover 6** is, for most of the NFL, quarter-quarter-half, with the quarters toward the
  strength. But in Nick Saban's vocabulary "6" has been a Cover 3 with a *weak rotation*: at the
  snap the safety on the side away from the offense's strength comes down toward the line, and the
  other safety goes to the deep middle. His "7" is a whole family of split-field, quarters-based
  match coverages built from a separate call for each side
  ([Cover 7](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cover-7-match-family) is defined in
  [Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage](06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd)).[^soran]
- **[Cover 8](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cover-8)** is rare in charting and has no standard
  meaning. In Vic Fangio's system, the most copied NFL defense of the last decade, Cover 8 is the
  same quarters-and-half idea that most teams call Cover 6, with the halves swapped. The analyst
  Cody Alexander describes Fangio's version as putting the Cover 2 half toward the offense's
  passing strength and the quarters away from it, the mirror image of the usual Cover 6.[^fangio8]
  Other staffs use 8 for other calls entirely.
- **[Cover 9](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cover-9)** depends on whom you ask. Some NFL staffs
  use it for the weak-rotation Cover 3 that Saban calls 6: one film analyst described the 2022
  Seahawks as playing "a nickel cover-9 defense (cover-3 with safety rotation away from the nickel
  defender)."[^seattle9] Saban's 6 is someone else's 9, which is the dialect problem in one line.
  Others use 9 for Cover 3 match (the meaning drawn above), or for a split-field call. In the Madden
  video game it is the mirror image of Cover 6: quarters on one side and Cover 2 on the other,
  flipped.[^madden9]

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
Madden's play-call screen makes coverages look like a fixed menu: Cover 3 Sky, Cover 2 Man, Cover 6,
each with one diagram. Real NFL defenses don't call "Cover 3" and get one picture. A call is a word
or two in the team's own language, plus tags that adjust it to the formation, the down and the
opponent ("Cover 3, rotate weak, match the slot"), and the same word means different things in
different buildings. When a broadcaster or a charting service says "Cover 3," it's a *translation*
into the common numbering of what the defense actually called. And the call isn't fixed when the
huddle breaks. It comes from the sideline, usually through the
[helmet radio](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-helmet-radio) of one defender, and most defenses
carry automatic checks that change it once they see the formation or the motion (the 3x1 checks in
[Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage](06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd) are the
standard example). That's also why two careful charters can watch the same play and write down
different numbers, as the next chart shows.
:::

### How often you'll see each number

Two charting services have labelled every NFL dropback's coverage since 2018: Next Gen Stats, the
league's own tracking-data arm, through 2022, and FTN, a private football-data company that charts every
play from video, from 2023. Both sets of labels are published free through nflverse. Their labels give a rough sense of
how common each coverage is, and their disagreements are a lesson in dialects of their own.

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (coverage labels on NFL dropbacks, nflverse, 2018–2025)"
#| output: false
from gridiron.data import nfl, pbp

LABEL = {"COVER_0": "Cover 0", "COVER_1": "Cover 1", "COVER_2": "Cover 2", "2_MAN": "2-Man (Cover 5)",
         "COVER_3": "Cover 3", "COVER_4": "Cover 4 (quarters)", "COVER_6": "Cover 6", "COVER_9": "Cover 9"}


def labelled_dropbacks(season):
    """Regular-season dropbacks with a charted coverage label (nflverse pbp + participation)."""
    b = pbp([season], columns=["game_id", "play_id", "season_type", "qb_dropback"])
    b = b[(b["season_type"] == "REG") & (b["qb_dropback"] == 1)]
    part = nfl().load_participation([season]).to_pandas().rename(columns={"nflverse_game_id": "game_id"})
    m = b.merge(part[["game_id", "play_id", "defense_coverage_type"]], on=["game_id", "play_id"])
    m = m[m["defense_coverage_type"].notna()].copy()
    m["season"] = season
    return m


COV = pd.concat([labelled_dropbacks(s) for s in range(2018, 2026)], ignore_index=True)
COV["era"] = np.where(COV["season"] <= 2022, "2018–2022 (Next Gen Stats charting)", "2023–2025 (FTN charting)")
COV["label"] = COV["defense_coverage_type"].map(LABEL).fillna("Other (prevent, combo, blown)")
SHARE = (COV.groupby("era")["label"].value_counts(normalize=True).mul(100).unstack(0).fillna(0.0))
ORDER = ["Cover 0", "Cover 1", "Cover 2", "2-Man (Cover 5)", "Cover 3", "Cover 4 (quarters)", "Cover 6",
         "Cover 9", "Other (prevent, combo, blown)"]
SHARE = SHARE.reindex(ORDER)
N_ERA = COV.groupby("era").size()
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-coverage-mix
#| fig-cap: "Share of labelled regular-season dropbacks by coverage, as charted by Next Gen Stats (2018–2022, about 90,000 dropbacks) and by FTN (2023–2025, about 61,000). Cover 3 and Cover 1, the two one-high coverages, lead in both. Cover 9 exists only in the FTN labels, and the two services split the rest differently (FTN calls far more plays Cover 2 and fewer Cover 3), so compare coverages within a period, not across the break."
eras = list(SHARE.columns)
y = np.arange(len(ORDER))[::-1]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 3.9))
hgt = 0.38
for i, (era, col) in enumerate(zip(eras, (style.SERIES[0], style.SERIES[1]))):
    vals = SHARE[era].values
    ax.barh(y + (hgt / 2 if i == 0 else -hgt / 2), vals, height=hgt, color=col, label=era)
    for yy, v in zip(y + (hgt / 2 if i == 0 else -hgt / 2), vals):
        ax.text(v + 0.4, yy, f"{v:.1f}%" if v >= 0.05 else "—", va="center", fontsize=6.8, color=style.INK_2)
ax.set_yticks(y, ORDER, fontsize=8)
ax.set_xlabel("share of labelled dropbacks (%)", fontsize=8)
ax.set_xlim(0, max(SHARE.max()) * 1.15)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=7.5)
ax.legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=7.5)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Three things to take from the chart:

- **One-high still rules on an ordinary down.** In both periods Cover 3 and Cover 1 together
  account for more than half of the labelled dropbacks. Two-high has been growing (the Next Gen
  Stats split-safety rate above), but the two classic one-high coverages remain the foundation of
  most NFL defenses. Why, when the famous defenses of the last decade went two-high? Because the
  safety who isn't deep is an extra run defender in the box, which two-high gives up
  ([A First Look at Defense](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd)
  counts the boxes), and because Cover 1 and Cover 3 are the simplest coverages to teach and to play
  fast.
- **Cover 9 appears only from 2023**, because FTN uses the label and Next Gen Stats did not; the
  public data dictionary lists it without defining it, and at 1.5 to 2.5 percent of labelled
  dropbacks a season it's a niche call whatever it means.[^ftn]
- **The two charters disagree.** FTN labels far more dropbacks Cover 2 and far fewer Cover 3 than
  Next Gen Stats did. Even on the same season they differ: for 2025, Next Gen Stats' own figures
  put Cover 2 at about 14 percent of plays, while FTN's labels put it above 20. Neither is "wrong":
  both are translating thousands of defensive calls into ten numbers, with different rules. That is the dialect problem in data form, and it's why
  [Tracking Data and the Big Data Bowl](../13-analytics-and-data/13-05-tracking-data-and-big-data-bowl.qmd)
  treats coverage labels as estimates, not facts.[^labels]

## Film room

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Seattle Seahawks 2013 — press Cover 3"}
Pete Carroll's Seattle defenses of the early 2010s, the "Legion of Boom," were built on the
simplest coverage in this chapter played with unusual corners. The base call was Cover 3: Earl
Thomas alone in the deep middle, Richard Sherman and Brandon Browner (then, late in 2013, Byron
Maxwell) in the deep outside thirds, and Kam Chancellor, the strong safety, rolled down as one of
the four underneath defenders. What made it look strange was that the corners *pressed*.
Tall, long-armed cornerbacks lined up on the receivers' noses and used Carroll's "step-kick", a
patient step and then a kick back to stay on the receiver's hip, which the players summarised as
"step for patience, kick for position."[^stepkick] It is a press-and-carry technique, not a bail:
the corner stays square, gets his hands on the receiver inside the 5-yard limit, and if the
receiver runs deep, runs *with* him up the sideline as if in man, inside his own deep third.
NFL.com described the scheme simply as a "press man, Cover Three defense."[^wesseling] It wasn't
press on every snap: against a side with a single receiver the corner pressed, and against a side
with two or more receivers he usually played off and bailed.[^brooks] In 2013 the defense led the
league in points allowed, yards allowed and takeaways, the first to lead all three since the 1985
Bears, and beat Denver 43–8 in Super Bowl XLVIII.[^sea2013]

**What to notice:** the corners' pre-snap alignment says man and the single high safety says MOFC.
At the snap, watch the corner's first steps (the jam) and then his path: running with the receiver
deep, but staying outside the middle third, which is Thomas's. The underneath defenders face the
quarterback like zone players, but by rule they carry receivers who run up the seams, so it's a
zone with match rules; analysts at the time described Seattle's corners as playing "press and
pattern match."[^bowen] [Cover 3](06-03-cover-3-family.qmd) builds Seattle's match version.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Tampa Bay Buccaneers 1996–2002 — spot-drop zone and eyes on the quarterback"}
Tony Dungy and Monte Kiffin's Buccaneers turned a two-deep zone into an identity. The
[Tampa 2](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tampa-2) was Cover 2 with a twist: the middle linebacker
ran deep down the middle of the field at the snap, closing the hole between the two deep safeties.
Dungy said its roots were in the 1970s Steelers ("My philosophy is really out of the 1975 Pittsburgh
Steelers playbook"), and in 2002, the season after Dungy left for Indianapolis, Kiffin's defense
finished first in the league in yards allowed and won Super Bowl XXXVII under Jon Gruden.[^tampa2] [Cover 2 and Tampa 2](06-04-cover-2-and-tampa-2.qmd) has the details.

**What to notice:** the defenders' drops. At the snap the underneath players turn and run to
spots, the hook defenders to the hashes, with their eyes on the quarterback, and then they break on
the ball together. It's spot-drop zone at heart, with one key match rule: the middle linebacker
doesn't just drop to a spot, he runs straight back and carries the inside receiver who runs up the
seam between the two safeties. Otherwise no defender chases a receiver; everyone faces the throw,
and receivers are tackled the moment they catch it.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Philadelphia Eagles 2024 — Vic Fangio's two-high match"}
Vic Fangio's defenses, from his Bears years (2015–18) through the 2024 Eagles, showed quarterbacks
the middle of the field open on snap after snap: two safeties deep, usually at the same depth
whatever the call, then a quarters coverage, a Cover 6 (his Cover 8), or a rotation to Cover 3 at
the snap. In his first season in Philadelphia the Eagles
allowed the fewest yards per game in the league (278.4) and the second-fewest points.[^eagles2024]
They won Super Bowl LIX 40–22, with their pass rush coming from four-man rushes.[^sblix] Fangio is
still the Eagles' defensive coordinator in 2026.

**What to notice:** before the snap, two safeties at 12 yards or more and corners off with eyes
inside, the same picture whatever is coming, which is the point: depth tells you little here. After
the snap, watch whether the safeties stay deep and read the slot receivers (quarters) or one of them
rotates down (a Cover 3 call disguised as two-high). The shell says "middle open" every time; the coverage changes
underneath it. The full story is the case study
[Fangio's Two-High Revolution and Macdonald's Answer](../12-case-studies/12-08-two-high-to-macdonald.qmd).
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it on Sunday: one or two?"}
For one quarter, on every passing down:

- **Before the snap, count the deep safeties.** One in the middle or two split wide? Say "closed"
  or "open" out loud *at the snap*. Then look at the details: deep and wide (toward the slot
  receivers) leans halves; shallower and tight to the hashes leans quarters. Many NFL teams hide
  this by lining every safety up at the same depth, so don't lean on it hard.
- **Look at one cornerback.** Press or off? Inside or outside shade? Eyes on the receiver or turned
  in to the quarterback? Press with eyes on the receiver leans man; off and turned in leans zone.
- **One second after the snap, check yourself.** Did the middle stay closed or open? Did a
  "two-high" safety drop down into the box or the hole? Did the corner run *with* his receiver, or
  turn and bail to a spot (Cover 3), or pedal and read the receiver in front of him (quarters)?
  Write down what it became.
- **On the replay, watch one underneath defender for one second.** To a spot (spot-drop), with a
  receiver from the start (man), or with a receiver after a beat (match)? Then find the ball: if a
  receiver was open, which zone was he in, and where were the nearest defender's eyes?

**On the broadcast camera.** The usual live shot is from high on the sideline, looking across the
field, so the offense moves left or right across your screen, and the two cornerbacks are at the top
and bottom edges. The safeties are often out of frame until the snap, or just at the edge, which is
why the analyst's "middle of the field closed" usually comes on the replay. A bail looks like a
corner at the top or bottom of the screen turning and running the same way as the receiver before
the receiver has reached him; press looks like two players colliding at the edge of the frame. The high, wide
replay angles (the closest a broadcast gets to the [All-22](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-all-22)
film coaches use) are the best place to make the call and check it.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: off corners, one safety, then the snap"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-offman
#| fig-cap: "Third-and-11, ball in the middle. Left, the pre-snap picture: one safety (FS) deep in the middle; both corners (CB) about 8 yards off with outside leverage; the nickel ($) and the strong safety (SS) about 5 yards deep, just inside the slot receivers. Right, the same play 1.3 seconds after the snap: H is running a shallow cross to the right, Y a short out. The corners and the two slot defenders are ringed."
def offman():
    pr = Play(spread(), nickel(FS=(14.5, 0.5), SS=(5.5, 7.4), NB=(5.0, -7.4), LCB=(7.8, -16.3),
                               RCB=(7.8, 16.3), MIKE=(4.5, 1.6), WILL=(4.5, -2.4)), los=40, to_go=11)
    pr.route("X", r.go(20.0))
    pr.route("Z", r.go(20.0))
    pr.route("H", [(0, 0), (2.0, -1.0), (3.0, -18.0)])
    pr.route("Y", r.out(5.0, 5.0))
    pr.block("RB", pts=[(0.6, 1.2)])
    pr.dropback(2.5)
    protect(pr)
    pr.drop("FS", (16.0, 0.5), speed=2.0)
    pr.drop("MIKE", (5.5, 1.2), speed=2.0)
    pr.drop("WILL", (6.8, -1.6), speed=2.5)
    set_track(pr, "LCB", [(0.5, 8.6, -16.0), (0.9, 9.4, -15.5), (1.5, 11.0, -15.4)])
    set_track(pr, "RCB", [(0.5, 8.6, 16.0), (0.9, 9.4, 15.5), (1.5, 11.0, 15.4)])
    # man: the $ follows H across the formation, the SS goes outside with Y
    set_track(pr, "NB", [(0.4, 4.5, -7.6), (0.8, 3.6, -6.0), (1.3, 3.0, -2.4), (2.0, 3.0, 3.0)])
    set_track(pr, "SS", [(0.4, 5.2, 8.0), (0.8, 4.8, 9.2), (1.3, 4.6, 12.4), (2.0, 4.6, 13.0)])
    return pr


pr1 = offman()
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.0))
for ax, t, ttl in zip(axes, (0.0, 1.3), ("Before the snap", "+1.3 s after the snap")):
    fld = moment(ax, pr1, t, (-22.0, 22.0), (-7.5, 18.5), rings=("LCB", "RCB", "NB", "SS"))
    panel_title(ax, ttl, fs=8.2)
    ruler(fld, pr1, fs=5.2, top=15)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8)
plt.show()
```

**Before the snap, what does this look like? After it, what is it really, and why would a defense
play it this way on third-and-11?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**It looks like Cover 3 and it's Cover 1, man coverage played from off alignments.** Before the snap
everything points to Cover 3: middle of the field closed, corners 8 yards off with outside leverage,
the slot defenders a few yards inside the slots like curl-flat players. A second later the
evidence overrules the hypothesis. The nickel has gone *across the formation* with H on his
shallow cross, and the strong safety has gone outside with Y. Zone defenders don't do that: a
curl-flat defender would let H run out of his area to the hook defender. When a slot defender
follows his receiver out of his own area within the first second, it's man. The corners, square
and staying on top of X and Z rather than turning and bailing to a landmark, agree.

Why off-man on third-and-11? Because the first job is to keep everything in front of the defenders
and short of the sticks, and a corner pressed on a receiver who only needs to run past 11 yards
risks being beaten deep. From off, he can give up the short throw and tackle it. The quarterback's
answer is the crosser: H is dragging his defender through traffic, and a deeper crossing route or
a rub would get a receiver past the sticks with a man defender trailing him.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: two safeties, close to the box"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-quarters
#| fig-cap: "Second-and-6, ball in the middle. Two safeties about 10 yards deep, each just outside a hash and well inside a slot receiver; corners 7 to 8 yards off; the nickel ($) in the apex inside the left slot, the Mike (M) in the apex inside the tight end, the Will (W) over the ball. The safeties are ringed."
pr2 = Play(spread(), nickel(FS=(10.0, -4.5), SS=(10.0, 4.5), NB=(4.5, -6.8), LCB=(7.5, -15.8),
                            RCB=(7.5, 15.8), MIKE=(4.8, 5.6), WILL=(4.5, -0.8)), los=40, to_go=6)
pr2.highlight("FS", "SS")
fld = draw(pr2, lateral=(-22, 22), window=(-7.5, 19.0))
widths(fld, pr2, -6.6)
plt.show()
```

**Closed or open? What coverage do the safeties' depth and width suggest, and where is this
defense thinnest against the pass?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Middle of the field open, and the shallow, tight safeties point to quarters (Cover 4).** Cover 2
safeties would usually be deeper (12 to 14 yards) and wider (out toward the slot receivers),
because each has half the field. These two are at 10 yards, near the hashes and well inside the
slots, the alignment of quarters safeties, who guard only the inside quarter deep and read the slot
receiver in front of them (#2). If #2 runs vertically, the safety covers him; that is who has Y
here. If #2 blocks or the play is a run, the safety comes downhill and becomes an extra run
defender. Count them: four linemen, two linebackers and two safeties are eight players who can
reach a run between the tackles, with the nickel in the apex as a ninth to the outside. That is why
defenses like quarters on early downs: two-high against the pass, with numbers against the run. One
caution: a disciplined NFL defense may line up exactly like this and play something else, or play
quarters from 13 yards, so the snap still has the last word.

The thin spot is **underneath and outside**. Four deep leaves three underneath, so short throws to
the outside receivers (hitches and quick outs in front of the off corners) and to the flats are
open, and a safety reading the run is vulnerable to play-action behind him. What's hard is the
deep ball: four defenders in four narrow lanes. ([Quarters](06-05-quarters-and-match.qmd) shows
how its match rules handle the slot routes.)
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: third-and-6, everybody tight"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-cover1
#| fig-cap: "Third-and-6. One safety (FS) 15 yards deep in the middle. Both corners (CB) pressed about a yard off the outside receivers, square to them; the nickel ($) pressed on the left slot; the strong safety (SS) 4 yards off the tight end Y in the right slot; the two linebackers inside. The corners and the free safety are ringed."
pr3 = Play(spread(), nickel(FS=(15.0, 0.0), SS=(4.0, 8.4), NB=(1.6, -8.4), LCB=(1.3, -15.7),
                            RCB=(1.3, 15.7), MIKE=(4.5, 1.2), WILL=(4.5, -2.4)), los=40, to_go=6)
pr3.highlight("FS", "LCB", "RCB")
fld = draw(pr3, lateral=(-22, 22), window=(-7.5, 19.0))
widths(fld, pr3, -6.6)
plt.show()
```

**Man or zone? What is the defense most likely playing, which routes should the quarterback
like, and what does the 5-yard rule have to do with it?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Most likely man coverage with one deep safety: Cover 1.** Middle of the field closed, and every
receiver has a defender tight on him: corners pressed and square, the nickel pressed on H, the
strong safety close on Y. The linebackers likely "have the back": one of them covers the running
back man to man if he runs a route, and the other, with nobody to cover, sits in the hole as a rat
or joins the rush. On third-and-6 that's a common call: the defense wants every short throw
contested.

The quarterback should like **routes that beat man**: quick slants and outs that win at the break,
crossing routes and rubs that drag defenders through traffic ([Dropback Concepts](../04-the-passing-game/04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd)'s
mesh), and a back-shoulder throw against a corner in trail. He should not expect receivers to
"find a soft spot and sit," because there are no soft spots in man: sitting down next to your
defender just makes the throw harder. And the 5-yard rule is the receiver's friend: all of the
corners' contact has to happen inside 5 yards. A receiver who wins his release has a defender
chasing him with his back to the quarterback, and only the free safety behind them. If the pressed corners bail at
the snap, it was a disguised zone and the quarterback has to adjust after the snap.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **Every coverage is a decision about how many defenders to put deep.** Thirds (three deep, four
  under), halves (two deep, five under) and quarters (four deep, three under) each buy something
  and give something up; with four rushers, every defender added deep is one taken from underneath.
- **The underneath map is flat, curl, hook and hole.** There are always more areas than defenders,
  so zone players are taught to cover two areas each, and they drop to landmarks so the gaps are
  the planned size on every play.
- **How a defender lines up is a message.** Press contests timing and needs help deep; off coverage
  gives a cushion to protect against the deep ball; a press-bail makes zone look like man. Leverage
  tells you where his help is, and the 5-yard rule means all of press's contact has to happen in
  the first 5 yards.
- **There are three ways to guard a receiver:** spot-drop zone (run to a place, watch the
  quarterback), pattern matching (start as zone, pick up receivers by rule) and man (go with one
  receiver from the snap). Watch one underneath defender for one second and you can usually tell
  which.
- **Read the middle of the field.** Closed (one safety in the post) means Cover 1 or Cover 3 most of
  the time; open means a two-high coverage. Safety depth and width, corner depth and leverage, and
  slot alignment narrow it down, and the snap confirms or overturns it.
- **Coverage numbers count deep defenders through Cover 4, then become names.** Cover 6, 7, 8 and 9
  mean different things in different playbooks, and even charting services disagree.

The rule text, the pocket condition and the automatic first down, as summarised for fans with a league umpire: "Football 101: What Is Illegal Contact?", PhiladelphiaEagles.com (Oct. 12, 2014): https://www.philadelphiaeagles.com/news/football-101-what-is-illegal-contact-13967625 ("Beyond the five-yard zone, if the player who receives the snap remains in the pocket with the ball, a defender cannot initiate contact with a receiver who is attempting to evade him"). The automatic first down still applies in 2026: a Lions proposal to remove it for illegal contact and defensive holding failed in 2025 (SI, "Lions' defensive holding proposal does not pass": https://www.si.com/nfl/lions/news/lions-defensive-holding-proposal-does-not-pass), and the 2026 rule changes did not touch it.
